title: Starting again
hookLine: refugee Sikh families rebuild from nothing in Delhi, East Punjab and beyond

lines: A CART, A NEEDLE, A SCHOOL UNDER A TREE.
cards: A refugee train pulls into Delhi in the autumn of 1947, and a family climbs down with a bundle of clothes, a few pots and a brass water jug from home. Back home they had a farm, or a shop, or a house with a courtyard.
Now they have a tent in a refugee camp and a number on a list. The father finds a cart and sells whatever he can buy cheap that morning. The mother takes in sewing.
The children go to school under a tree. It will take years; some families will tell you it took a generation.

teach.b: In Delhi there was Kingsway Camp; near Kurukshetra, a huge camp of tents held a city's worth of people. Hindu and Sikh refugees from the west lived in them for months, some for years. Then the building began.
Whole new neighborhoods went up in Delhi for refugee families, and you can still hear Punjabi from the older shops there.
In East Punjab, families who had left farms were given land against what they'd lost, often less, and often worse, than what they left behind. They cleared it and planted anyway.
Many moved on again, to other cities, and later across the world. Underneath all of this is a Sikh word you learned early on the path: chardi kala.
Chardi means rising, climbing; kala is spirit, strength. Rising spirits, an unbeaten heart. It's said at the end of every Ardas, and it doesn't mean pretending things are fine.
The families of 1947 grieved; many never spoke about what they saw.
Chardi kala is grief and getting up at the same time. It sits beside another old teaching, kirat karni, earning an honest living with your own hands. A cart is honest work.
So is a needle, or a small shop. Families still tell of a grandfather who started over late in life with nothing but that. Today's line has one extra word: again.
Chardi kala isn't a mood you find once. It's something you choose again, the next morning, and the next.

how: Sikhs close the Ardas by asking for chardi kala, rising spirits, and many families from Partition speak of it together with kirat karni, honest work, when they tell how they rebuilt.

o: forgetting the past so it can't hurt anymore
returning home once the old land is given back
rebuilding from nothing, with rising spirits each day

games.q: the words of starting again — tap the pairs.

s: refugee farmers got back the same land they lost
land in East Punjab was given against what was lost, and was often smaller and poorer.
chardi kala means pretending everything is fine
it is grief and getting up at the same time: rising spirits, not a forced smile.
new neighborhoods were built in Delhi for refugee families
whole colonies went up for families from the west, and many still carry that history.

games.q: you've arrived in Delhi in 1947 with almost nothing. a neighbor in the camp offers a cart. what do many families do?
o: wait in the camp until the old land is returned.
take whatever honest work there is and start again.
leave the city and go back west.
games.why: families tell of carts, sewing and small shops: kirat karni, honest work, and chardi kala, starting over.

practice: Think of something you let go of when life got hard: a walk you used to take, a letter you meant to write, a few lines of reading.
Don't scold yourself about why it stopped; just pick it up in your mind, the way you'd pick up a tool. Find the smallest possible first step, and let that decision settle with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Starting again. Refugee families of 1947 rebuilt from nothing, in tents, carts and new fields, with chardi kala: rising spirits, chosen again each day.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: chardi kala, rising spirits; said at the close of every Ardas.

carryVoice: Your line: chardi kala, again. A cart, a needle, a small shop: that's how it began. See you tomorrow.
